newsitem.title: UK: Bulgaria Brady rise stops, Russia firm.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Brady rise stops, Russia firm.

text.p: Bulgaria's latest surge on the emerging debt market on government promises to meet Brady bond repayments this month came to a halt on Wednesday and traders said the country's future remains very uncertain.
Russia was slightly firmer but the market in general remains extremely wary of a possible U.S. interest rate hike which would be certain to hit Bradys.
"Emerging markets have been relatively resilient but have not managed to decouple from the U.S.," Bank of America analyst Richard Gray said.

To retain insulation from the U.S. market, investors should buy uncollateralised floating-rate Bradys with a high running yield against fixed paper, at least until there is clear evidence of a U.S. economic weakening, he added.
Bulgaria's Tuesday rise was short-lived and several traders said investment in the Bradys was best limited to options until economic prospects there become clearer.

The key focus is whether Sofia will win over the International Monetary Fund and so stand a chance of bringing in desperately needed external finance to help it meet its debt obligations for the year.
Bulgarian Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov on Tuesday promised to pay the $135.5 million Brady coupon payments due on January 28.
He also said the establishment of a currency board, a requirement of the IMF, could be achieved by end-month.
Once that is set up, Bulgarian Bradys -- which currently have by far the widest spreads over U.S. Treasuries in the market -- should rise, one trader said.
But others warned that an IMF agreement was not a certainty and wondered if Sofia would be able to sustain a currency board if it did establish one.
Traders said that in general most emerging debt investors were holding back, waiting to see what impact U.S. economic data, including payroll figures on Friday, had on U.S. Treasuries.
